turns.prompt:
You are given two attached CSV files describing perovskite solar cells as
complete devices — `substrate` (glass + transparent electrode), `etl`
(electron-transport layer stack), `htl` (hole-transport layer stack),
`backcontact` (metal / carbon back electrode), `deposition` (absorber
deposition procedure; `>>` separates steps). Every candidate below uses the
same MAPbI3 absorber in the same n-i-p (regular) architecture; they differ
only in the remaining columns. Each row is a device CONFIGURATION whose
efficiency is the median over at least 3 independently fabricated cells, so
it is a reproducible recipe rather than a single champion cell:
  - b3_pvk_stack_train.csv: 300 configurations with the measured power
    conversion efficiency (%).
  - b3_pvk_stack_pool.csv: 100 CANDIDATE configurations whose power
    conversion efficiency (%) was NOT measured, columns `candidate_id` and
    the same device columns.

Using the training data, select the 5 candidates with the HIGHEST power
conversion efficiency (%).

Reason from the device physics — band alignment and selectivity of the
transport layers, interface recombination, contact chemistry and the film
quality the process is likely to give — then end your answer with an
explicit ranked list of candidate_ids, best first, e.g. "Final: c901, c902,
c903, c904, c905".
turns.answer_text:
My predicted top five are **c064, c005, c017, c068, and c043**. I prioritize candidates resembling the highest-performing training configurations, using interface selectivity, contact chemistry, and processing to judge the differences. These are predictions of configuration-level median efficiency—not measured efficiencies or a guaranteed ordering.

| Rank | Candidate | Training evidence and device-physics rationale |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | **c064** | **TiO2-c / SnO2-np / Spiro-MeOTAD / Au.** The closest high-performing training example uses the same ETL and HTL, but Ag and spin-coating followed by dip-coating, and reaches **20.85%**. Another TiO2-c/SnO2/Spiro device reaches **17.47%** with spin-coating. The compact TiO2 layer provides coverage and hole blocking; the SnO2 overlayer offers a favorable electron-extraction interface. Spiro/Au provides an established hole-selective contact. The changed deposition procedure makes transferring the 20.85% result directly unjustified, but this remains the strongest ETL-family match. |
| **2** | **c005** | **TiO2-c / PCBM-60 / PCDTBT8 / MoO3 / Au.** A particularly close training configuration—with FTO instead of ITO and **PCDTBT1 instead of PCDTBT8**—achieves **19.35%** using the same two-step deposition sequence. PCBM can improve electron selectivity and passivate the oxide/perovskite interface, while MoO3 can improve hole extraction into Au. The polymer substitution is the principal uncertainty: related names do not guarantee identical energy levels, mobility, or film quality. |
| **3** | **c017** | **Fullerene-based ETL / doped TaTm HTL / Ag, co-evaporated.** Apart from capitalization differences in material labels, the training set contains essentially this configuration with **Au**, achieving **17.9%**. That is unusually direct support. The fullerene electron contact and doped molecular hole contact provide complementary selectivity, while co-evaporation offers controlled film formation. Ag introduces more concern about iodide reaction and migration than Au, so I would not assume an improvement over that reference. |
| **4** | **c068** | **SnO2-np / TiO2-np / PTAA / Au–MoO3.** The training set supports both the SnO2/PTAA combination (**18.19%**) and complementary SnO2/TiO2 electron-contact stacks (**16.54%** with Spiro). PTAA is an effective electron-blocking hole transporter. The mixed-oxide ETL could improve coverage and extraction, although its benefit depends on nanoparticle connectivity and interfacial defects. The listed Au/MoO3 sequence should not automatically be treated as equivalent to MoO3/Au. |
| **5** | **c043** | **TiO2-c / TiO2-mp / DAHI / Spiro-MeOTAD / Au.** This retains a well-established mesoporous electron-contact stack and Spiro/Au hole contact, while adding an interlayer with potential to reduce interfacial recombination. The training set shows that modifying the perovskite/Spiro interface can be valuable: **PMMA/Spiro reaches 18.01%**, and **PbS-QDs/Spiro reaches 18.63%** in a compact-TiO2 device. This is the least certain selection because DAHI itself is unrepresented; its benefit requires passivation without an excessive hole-extraction barrier. |

The main uncertainty is **how much benefit transfers between different interfacial modifiers or polymer variants**. I therefore give more weight to the close device-level matches than to unfamiliar materials that merely sound promising.

Final: c064, c005, c017, c068, c043
